sense: how old someone is; a time of life

evidence: Quint. 1 pr. 6: cujus prīma aetās manifestum jam ingeniī lūmen ostendit
terms.comment: Someone’s age and a stage of life: prīma aetās, early years. It is also a lifetime and an age of history (see life, generation).

terms.gloss: at that age, of that age
terms.grammar: fixed phrase: the neuter id with a genitive, used like an adjective or adverb; so hoc aetātis, at this age
evidence: Cic. Fam. 6.20.3: id aetātis jam sumus, we have now reached that time of life (Lewis & Short s.v. aetās)
terms.comment: The phrase does not change with its noun: homō id aetātis, a man of that age; id aetātis sumus, we are of an age. So also id temporis, at that time.

terms.grammar: participle agreeing with the person, with the accusative of the number of years
evidence: Cic. de Or. 3.74: annōs nātus ūnum et vīgintī (Lewis & Short s.v. nāscor)
terms.comment: The ordinary way to state an age. With a noun the genitive also serves: puer trium annōrum, a boy of three (see how old are you?, a man of).

terms.grammar: present participle of agō with an ordinal in the accusative
evidence: Liv. 40.6.4: trīcēsimum annum agēns (Lewis & Short s.v. trīcēsimus)
Cic. Sen. 32: quārtum agō annum et octōgēsimum
terms.comment: “Spending the …th year”: the ordinal counts the year one is in, so decimum quīntum annum agēns is strictly one who is fourteen, in his fifteenth year, though Traupman renders it “at age fifteen”.

terms.grammar: comparative agreeing with the person; quam may be left out without changing the case
evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 39: annōs nātus mājor quadrāgintā, over forty years old (Lewis & Short s.v. magnus)
Nep. Reg. 2.3: mājor annōs sexāgintā nātus dēcessit (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: sī hominem id aetātis in tam longō sermōne diūtius retinuisset
phrases.english: if he had kept a man of that age any longer in so long a conversation

phrases.latin: quattuor et vīgintī fermē annōs nātus

phrases.english: I am in my eighty-fourth year

sources: The examples are from the Latīnitās loci collections and the note on quantity words, checked there against the texts; Lewis & Short’s citations are marked.
